Debug logging from the gateway produces about four terabytes a month, ninety percent of it from successful health checks and cache hits that nobody has ever searched for. Introduce sampling at the collector so that routine entries are kept at one in fifty while everything at warning or above, and every entry belonging to a trace that ended in an error, is kept in full.

Sampling a trace consistently is the hard part. If each service decides independently, the surviving fragments rarely line up. The collector therefore decides by hashing the trace identifier, so that every service keeps or drops the same traces, and a tail rule keeps traces whose root span reports an error even when the head decision would have dropped them. The tail rule needs the collector to hold spans in memory for up to thirty seconds before deciding, which is why the collectors move to larger instances with a memory limit and a drop-oldest policy under pressure.

Fields that make an entry interesting are configured per service in a rules file: status codes of five hundred and above, durations over a second, and any entry containing the word retry. The rules file is validated in the pipeline by replaying a day of sample logs through the new rules and printing how many entries each would keep.

A quiet failure mode to guard against: if the collector crashes and restarts, in-memory spans are lost, and traces that were about to be kept disappear. We accept that loss but count it, with a metric of spans dropped on restart, so that a crash loop is visible instead of looking like reduced traffic.

Billing impact is expected to be a reduction of about sixty percent of ingest volume, which should pay for the larger collectors several times over.
acceptanceCriteria: Routine entries are kept at one in fifty
Warnings, errors and traces with an error root are kept in full
All services keep or drop the same traces
Per-service rules are validated by replaying sample logs
Spans lost on collector restart are counted in a metric

comments.body: Replay of Tuesday's logs through the draft rules keeps 38 percent of entries, within the estimate.
Memory per collector peaks at 11 GB with the 30 second tail window; instance type bumped.

items.title: Propagate trace identifiers through queue messages
items.description:
Traces break at every queue. A request enters the gateway, enqueues a message, and the worker that handles it starts a fresh trace, so the story of one order is spread across unrelated entries. Carry the trace and span identifiers in message headers, and make the shared worker library read them and start its span as a child of the producer's span.

The standard header format is used so that third-party libraries understand it. Workers that pull messages in batches create one span per message, linked to the batch span, because a single parent cannot describe a batch.

Retries must keep the original trace, with the retry count as an attribute, so that a message that failed three times shows up as one trace with four attempts and not four separate ones.

Dead-letter queues are the exception that surprised us during testing. A message is moved to the dead-letter queue by the broker itself, and the broker does not copy custom headers when it dead-letters after the visibility timeout expires, only when the consumer rejects explicitly. Messages that die by timeout therefore lose their trace. Workers now write the trace identifiers into the message body envelope as a fallback and the replay tool reads either location.

Rollout order matters: producers first, because workers that find no header simply start a new trace, which is today's behaviour, while a worker deployed before producers would add nothing. Each service moves to the new library version in the order given in the epic's checklist.
acceptanceCriteria: Workers continue the producer's trace
Batches create linked spans per message
Retries keep the original trace with an attempt count
Dead-lettered messages keep their trace identifiers
Trace headers use the standard format

items.title: Log lines appear out of order because collectors use receive time
items.description:
Entries from the same request show up in the wrong order in the viewer when two services log within a few milliseconds of each other. The collector stamps entries with the time it received them, so network jitter reorders them. Use the timestamp set by the emitter, and only fall back to receive time when the emitter's is missing or more than ten minutes away from it.

A secondary symptom is entries dated slightly in the future when an emitter's clock is ahead, which makes the viewer's live tail jump. Clamping emitter timestamps to the receive time plus a small tolerance fixes that without trusting a wildly wrong clock.
items.reproSteps: Make a request that passes through the gateway and the orders service and search for its request id. Entries from the orders service sometimes appear before the gateway's first entry.

comments.body: Clock drift on two build servers was 40 seconds; time synchronisation was misconfigured there.

items.title: Add an emitter timestamp field to the shared logging library
items.description:
The library already writes time, but under a field name that the collector does not read. Rename it to the agreed field and keep the old one for one release.

Mixed-mode logging, in which some services emit the new field and some the old, must work for the length of the migration, so the collector looks for the new field first and falls back to the old one, counting how often it falls back as a progress measure.

items.title: ログの保持期間を90日に短縮する
items.description:
現在、すべてのサービスのログは1年間保持されていますが、実際に検索されるのは直近の2週間分がほとんどで、30日より古い記録を開くことはほぼありません。保管費用が月ごとに増えているため、保持期間を90日に短縮します。

ただし、監査対象の記録（決済と認証に関するもの）は法令上の理由から1年間の保持が必要なので、別のバケットに分け、従来どおりの期間を維持します。移行は、まず新しい保持設定を監査対象外のログにだけ適用し、1か月様子を見てから古いデータを削除する順で進めます。削除の前に、利用者に告知を出すことも手順に含めます。

保持期間の設定はインフラのコードで管理し、変更はレビューを経て適用します。削除対象の件数と容量は、実行前に一覧で確認できるようにします。
acceptanceCriteria: 監査対象外のログが90日で削除される
決済と認証の記録は1年間保持される
削除前に告知が行われる

comments.body: 費用の試算では、短縮後は保管料がおよそ半分になる見込みです。
監査対象のログを分けるバケットは、決済チームと認証チームの両方の承認を得てから作成します。

items.title: Archive search results to a shared notebook
items.description:
Removed: engineers asked for a button to save search results into a notebook. The log viewer vendor ships an equivalent feature, so we will not build our own.

The vendor feature can export a saved search into a shared notebook. Engineers who asked for it were shown the vendor's version in a demo and agreed it was enough. No code was written for the original idea.

items.title: On-call tooling
items.description:
The tools that wake someone up, tell them what is wrong, and help them fix it, with the aim that a page contains enough information to act on.

Most of what makes a page painful is missing context, not missing technology. A good page names the service, says what the alert measures, shows the graph, and links to the runbook, so the first five minutes are spent acting rather than hunting for these.

items.title: Route pages by service ownership
items.description:
Pages currently go to a single rotation for everything, so the person on call at three in the morning is asked about services they have never seen. Read ownership from the service catalogue and route each alert to the rotation of the owning team, with the platform rotation as a fallback for anything unowned.

The catalogue entry for a service lists the owning team, the escalation policy and the severity mapping. Alerts carry a service label set by the monitoring rules; an alert without the label is routed to the platform rotation and annotated as unowned, which gives a natural pressure to fix missing labels.

Escalation: if the primary does not acknowledge within ten minutes, page the secondary; after another ten, page the team lead; for severity one, page the incident commander rotation immediately in parallel.

Holiday and leave handling is separate. The on-call calendar shows who is covering, and the routing tool must read overrides from it, so a swap agreed in the calendar changes who receives the page without anyone editing the routing rules.

Migration approach: run the new routing in shadow for two weeks, sending a silent copy to the new target and comparing it with who actually handled the page. Where the copy would have gone to a different person than the one who ended up resolving it, the catalogue entry is likely wrong, and we fix the catalogue before cutting over.

One restriction to remember: alert rules created through the old interface cannot carry labels, so they are migrated to the rules repository first, and the interface is made read-only afterwards.
acceptanceCriteria: Alerts go to the rotation of the owning team
Unowned alerts go to the platform rotation and are annotated
Escalation follows 10 minute steps; severity one pages the incident commander at once
Calendar overrides change the recipient
Shadow mode compares routing with who resolved the page

comments.body: Service catalogue completeness is 83 percent; the missing entries are mostly old batch jobs.

items.title: Attach the matching runbook to every page
items.description:
Alerts carry a runbook link field; most are empty. Add a check to the rules repository that fails when a paging alert has no runbook link or the link returns an error, and ship a template runbook with the sections symptom, impact, first checks and escalation.

The check fetches each link with a short timeout and accepts only an ordinary successful response, so a runbook that has been moved gets noticed. The template includes a section on how to tell whether the problem is customer-visible, because that decides how urgent everything else is.

comments.body: Of 214 paging alerts, 61 have a working runbook link today.

items.title: The same incident pages three people through three alert rules
items.description:
A database failover triggers separate alerts from the service, the queue consumer and the synthetic checks, each paging the on-call. Group alerts that share a service label and fire within five minutes into a single page, with the others listed as related in its description. Grouping must never delay a severity one page.

Grouping should be visible in the page itself: the first alert becomes the page title, the others are listed beneath with times, and acknowledging the page acknowledges all of them. If an alert joins a group after acknowledgement, a note is added to the existing incident rather than paging again.
items.reproSteps: Trigger a database failover in staging with paging enabled. Three pages arrive within two minutes.

comments.body: Last quarter's failover paged four people from separate rules within ninety seconds.

items.title: Guía de recuperación tras una caída del clúster
items.description:
Escribir y ensayar una guía paso a paso para levantar de nuevo la plataforma cuando el clúster principal deja de responder por completo. La última vez que ocurrió, la recuperación llevó más de tres horas porque cada persona recordaba una parte distinta del orden correcto: primero la red y los certificados, después la base de datos, luego los servicios de identidad y, por último, las aplicaciones.

La guía debe incluir los comandos exactos, quién puede ejecutarlos, cómo comprobar que cada fase ha terminado y qué hacer si una fase falla. Una vez al trimestre se hará un simulacro en el entorno de pruebas con un cronómetro, y el resultado se anotará al final del documento.
acceptanceCriteria: La guía cubre las cuatro fases con comandos exactos
Se realiza un simulacro trimestral con tiempo medido

items.title: Build a mobile app for the on-call rotation
items.description:
Removed. The paging vendor's own app covers acknowledging and escalating, and a custom client would need its own release process.

The decision was made after a short review of what a client would have to do: push notifications that bypass silent mode, secure authentication, offline handling and an app store release process. The vendor's app already provides these, and our users are already familiar with it.

items.title: Internal command-line tool
items.description:
One command for the things engineers do every day: log in to the cloud, open a shell in a service, start a stopped development machine, tail logs and check a deploy.

The tool is a single binary with subcommands, distributed through the package manager. It talks to the same internal APIs as the dashboards and holds no state of its own beyond the cached tokens and a small completion cache, so that reinstalling it is always safe.

items.title: Single sign-on login that works in a terminal without a browser
items.description:
The tool's login command opens a browser tab and listens on a local port for the callback. That fails over remote shells and inside containers where there is no browser and no way to reach the port. Support the device authorisation flow: the tool prints a short code and a URL, the person approves on any device, and the tool polls until it receives a token.

Tokens are stored in the operating system's secure store where one exists and in a file with owner-only permissions otherwise. The refresh token lasts a working week; the access token lasts an hour and is renewed silently, so people see a login prompt about once a week.

Commands run in scripts need a non-interactive path. A service identity can be supplied by an environment variable holding a short-lived token, and the tool never prompts when it is set, failing with a clear error if the token is expired.

The polling interval comes from the server, and the tool must obey the slow-down response by adding five seconds to its interval, since ignoring it leads to rate limiting that looks like a hang. We found this in testing when two engineers behind the same office address were both polling at one-second intervals and the identity provider started returning errors for both.

Logout removes stored tokens and calls the revocation endpoint. A command to show who you are logged in as, with the expiry time, makes support questions easy to answer.

Testing matrix for the release: macOS with the keychain, Linux with and without a secret service daemon, Windows with the credential manager, and a minimal container image with only a home directory. The file fallback prints a one-time notice that tokens are stored unencrypted with owner-only permissions.
acceptanceCriteria: Login works over SSH and in containers using a printed code
Tokens are stored in the secure store or an owner-only file
Scripts can authenticate with an environment variable token
The tool honours the slow-down response while polling
Logout revokes the token

items.title: Shell completion for commands and service names
items.description:
Generate completion scripts for bash, zsh and fish, including dynamic completion of service names fetched from the catalogue and cached for ten minutes so that tab presses are instant.

Completion data for services is fetched with a hidden subcommand that returns plain lines, so shells that cannot run the binary still work with a static list. Failures in the fetch fall back silently to the cached list, since an error message in the middle of typing is worse than a stale suggestion.

comments.body: Zsh completion for service names works; fish still needs its own quoting rules.

items.title: Colour codes appear as raw text in the Windows terminal
items.description:
The status table shows sequences such as an escape bracket followed by numbers around every cell in the older Windows console. The tool should detect whether the output is a terminal that supports colour, honour the no-colour environment variable, and enable virtual terminal processing where the console allows it.

The no-colour convention is a plain environment variable with any non-empty value, and the tool should also turn colour off automatically when output is redirected to a file or a pipe. Tests run the status command with each combination and compare against golden outputs.
items.reproSteps: Run the status command in the legacy Windows console host (not the newer terminal application). The table is full of literal escape sequences.

comments.body: Reproduced in the legacy console only. The new terminal renders colours correctly.

items.title: Update the help text and add examples for every command
items.description:
Go through each command and make sure the description, flags and one realistic example are accurate. Add a test that fails when a command has no example.

Examples should use the fake service names from the sandbox catalogue so that people can paste them and see something useful. The test reads the command definitions and fails for a missing example, which has already found three undocumented flags.

items.title: Self-update check on every invocation
items.description:
Removed. Checking for a new version on each run slowed the tool and annoyed people in scripts. Updates now arrive through the package manager and a weekly notice in chat.

The weekly chat notice lists the newest version and a link to the changelog. Nothing in this item shipped, so no code needs reverting. A short note in the handbook explains how to upgrade through the package manager.
